questions.prompt: How can conditional requests help prevent a lost update?
options: Use Cache-Control: public for all private account data.
Ignore validators and let the last request always overwrite newer state.
Use a 304 response to confirm that a state-changing write succeeded.
Return an ETag and require a matching If-Match value for the update; reject a stale precondition.
questions.answer_key: Return an ETag and require a matching If-Match value for the update; reject a stale precondition.
questions.explanation: Return an ETag and require a matching If-Match value for the update; reject a stale precondition. This is especially relevant to “Cache-Control Directives” because the API contract must remain explicit and reviewable.

questions.prompt: For the lesson “Cache-Control Directives”, which check provides the strongest practical evidence?
options: Run one happy-path call and skip invalid, denied, and failure scenarios.
Test against production records so the exercise cannot be repeated safely.
Use current and stale validators in concurrent updates and confirm stale writes fail.
Rely on a code review comment without running any representative check.
questions.answer_key: Use current and stale validators in concurrent updates and confirm stale writes fail.
questions.explanation: A useful check is repeatable, tied to an observable contract, and includes an important negative or boundary scenario.

questions.prompt: Which review warning is most relevant to “Cache-Control Directives”?
options: The API avoids exposing internal secrets and personal data.
Stale writes overwrite newer state or shared caches expose personalized data.
The expected behavior and relevant failure cases are documented.
A representative test can reproduce the result.
questions.answer_key: Stale writes overwrite newer state or shared caches expose personalized data.
questions.explanation: This finding weakens a core API guarantee and should be treated as a design or release issue, not only a style concern.
